Secret class class Secret(value: str | None = None) Categories: credentials Reference to a secret value, used for credential fields. A Secret is either hydrated -- Secret("hunter2"), whose value() returns the value -- or dehydrated -- Secret(), whose value() raises. None is the dehydrated sentinel and is never a valid value. It always serializes to the redacted marker ":secret:", so the value never lands in the serialized form and str(secret) is always redacted.

StrOrSecretSpec type_alias StrOrSecretSpec: Union[str, Secret] Resolved type: str | Secret Categories: credentials A connector field that accepts either a plain string or a Secret. Annotate a connection/source/destination field with it directly. Each value carries a marker so the two shapes are unambiguous on the wire: "str:<value>" -- a plain string (<value> may be empty); "secret:<value>" -- a secret carrying <value>; ":secret:" -- a secret with no value yet (resolved at run time). An unmarked string is rejected. After validation a plain arm is a str and a secret arm a Secret, so read the value with a normal str or with Secret.value() respectively. Connector code that must resolve either arm to a concrete value uses the connector-common _convert helper.

Write a table to a single Parquet file, one slot per path: @subscriber( destination=AzureBlobDest( paths=["exports/rows.parquet"], format=DestFileFormat.PARQUET, ), input_tables=["mycoll/rows"], ) def publish(rows: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return rows Write CSV and tune the writer through format_cfg, keyed by the DestFileFormat: @subscriber( destination=AzureBlobDest( paths=["exports/rows.csv"], format=DestFileFormat.CSV, format_cfg={ DestFileFormat.CSV: { "separator": ";", "include_header": True, }, }, ), input_tables=["mycoll/rows"], ) def publish(rows: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return rows

parameter pathsDestPathsSpec (list[str]) Target paths relative to the connection's base_path, one write slot per entry. Each path is relative (no leading /), must not end with /, and must not contain empty segments (//). Write a table with the replace disposition -- the first run creates it, later runs drop and recreate it (row count stays): @subscriber( destination=ClickHouseDest( tables=["cap_replace"], if_table_exists="replace", ), input_tables=["caps_input/cap_rows"], ) def out_replace(rows: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return rows Append rows with a wider schema and let ClickHouse evolve the table -- schema_evolution="iceberg" adds the new column rather than failing on the mismatch ("strict" would reject it): @subscriber( destination=ClickHouseDest( tables=["cap_evolve"], if_table_exists="append", schema_evolution="iceberg", ), input_tables=["caps_input/cap_evo_v2"], ) def evolve(rows: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return rows

parameter tablesClickHouseTableNamesSpec (list[str]) Target table names (non-empty), one write slot per entry. Each is a 1- or 2-part name (table or database.table); backtick-quote a part for special characters.
parameter if_table_existsIfTableExistsSpec (Literal['append', 'replace']) "append" (the default) adds rows; "replace" overwrites the table.
parameter schema_evolutionSchemaEvolutionSpec (Literal['strict', 'iceberg']) "strict" (the default) rejects schema changes; "iceberg" applies Iceberg-style schema deltas.
parameter dest_cfgDestCfgSpec | None (Mapping[Literal['clickhouse.logging_level'], Any] | None) Optional connector config; the only supported key is clickhouse.logging_level.
method validate def validate() Cross-field validation: tables must be non-empty. Called by the framework; raises ClickHouseValidateException.

class class MongoDBDest( collections_with_ids: CollectionsWithIdsSpec, if_collection_exists: IfTableExistsSpec = 'append', use_trxs: bool = False, docs_per_trx: int = 1000, maintain_order: bool = False, update_existing: bool = True, fail_on_duplicate_key: bool = True, log_intermediate_files: bool = False, dest_cfg: DestCfgSpec | None = None, ) Bases: Dest Categories: destination MongoDB destination for @subscriber -- one slot per collection.

Append documents, letting MongoDB auto-generate _id (the id field is None): @subscriber( destination=MongoDBDest( collections_with_ids=[("cap_append", None)], ), input_tables=["caps_input/cap_rows"], ) def publish(rows: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return rows Upsert on a natural key -- code becomes each document's _id, so re-runs update the same documents instead of inserting duplicates: @subscriber( destination=MongoDBDest( collections_with_ids=[("cap_upsert", "code")], update_existing=True, ), input_tables=["caps_input/cap_rows"], ) def upsert(rows: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return rows

parameter collections_with_idsCollectionsWithIdsSpec (list[tuple[str, str | None]]) List of (collection, id_field) pairs, one write slot per entry. collection is the target collection, optionally qualified as <database>.<collection>; a bare <collection> targets the database named in the connection URI (a name up to 235 bytes, no NUL or $, not starting with system.). id_field is the document field used as the unique id, e.g. ("mydb.users", "user_id"); pass None (e.g. ("mydb.logs", None)) to let MongoDB auto-generate _id. An id_field may not be empty, contain . or NUL, or start with $.
parameter if_collection_existsIfTableExistsSpec (Literal['append', 'replace']) "append" (default) leaves existing documents in place; "replace" drops the collection first.
parameter use_trxsbool When true, each batch of docs_per_trx documents is wrapped in a MongoDB transaction (requires a replica set).
parameter docs_per_trxint Max documents per write batch / transaction (default 1000; must be greater than 0).
parameter maintain_orderbool When true, documents are inserted in input order (slower but deterministic server-side ordering).

parameter update_existingbool When true, documents whose id already exists are upserted (UpdateOne with upsert=True); when false, InsertOne is used and a collision aborts the batch. Ignored when id_field is None (auto-generated ids never collide).
parameter fail_on_duplicate_keybool When true, a duplicate-key error is re-raised; when false it is logged and the batch continues.

Data class class Data(df: Any, chunk_size: int | None = None) Categories: source One dataframe emitted by DataGenSrc, optionally chunked. A Data wraps a Polars or Pandas dataframe (a Pandas frame is converted to Polars on construction) plus a per-run chunk_size: chunk_size=None -- the whole dataframe is emitted on every run. chunk_size=N -- N rows are emitted per run, advancing an offset kept in the plugin's per-flow state; once the offset reaches the end the slot yields None (no more rows). On the wire a Data serialises to {"parquet": <base64>, "chunk_size": <int|null>}: the dataframe is written to parquet and base64-encoded on serialisation, and decoded back to a Polars frame on deserialisation so the plugin can materialise it to parquet for its output. Like Secret, it round-trips via its own pydantic core schema rather than the descriptor envelope.

property activebool True while the runtime wants the plugin to keep polling. The plugin loop should exit (cleanly) once this is False.

property first_stagebool True until the first batch has been staged + committed. The plugin uses it to decide where to seed its resume position: when first_stage is True nothing has been published yet, so seed from the source's configured initial values; otherwise a prior batch exists, so resume from stream_state (or, when the external system owns the offset, from the external system).

property stream_stateBasicDictSpec | None (dict[str, str | int | float | bool] | None) The per-flow resume state persisted by the most recent BasicDictSpec handed to stage. None when the last commit handed stage a CommitStateFn callable (a lambda) instead of a BasicDictSpec -- i.e. the external system owns the offset and Tabsdata keeps no state. Distinguish "first run" (nothing staged yet) via first_stage, not by this being None.
property flush_interval_minsint Maximum minutes the plugin may accumulate before it must stage, regardless of its own size/row thresholds.

StreamStageSrcPlugin class class StreamStageSrcPlugin Bases: SrcPlugin Categories: spi Hidden batch-side (publisher) source that ingests a stream stage's manifests. A StreamSrcPlugin only stages data (accumulates batches into storage and records each in a manifest); every StreamSrc needs a paired hidden SrcPlugin on the batch side to consume it, which must be this class or a subclass. Each execution consumes exactly one manifest -- the oldest unconsumed one -- advancing a per-flow cursor; it yields zero output slots when none remain. The manifest scan + ingest is fixed in read_in and must not be overridden; customise the ingested data (e.g. de-duplication) by overriding process_files instead. To register a customised variant, pair a StreamStageSrc subclass with this plugin in a SrcDef whose cardinality returns -1 (disables the slot-count check) and whose explorer is None.

LazyGroupBy class class LazyGroupBy(lgb, parent, by) Categories: aggregation Pending group-by over a TableFrame, produced by group_by. Obtain one from TableFrame.group_by(...), then call .agg(...) with reducing expressions such as col("v").sum(). The reduction shortcut methods (sum / min / max / mean / median / n_unique) reduce EVERY column and can fail on a table's hidden system columns; prefer agg(col(...).<reduction>()). count and len are always safe.

method agg def agg( *aggs: IntoExpr | Iterable[IntoExpr] = (), **named_aggs: IntoExpr = {}, ) -> TableFrame Reduce each group to one row using the given expressions. Each expression is a column reduction -- typically col(name) plus a reducer and an alias. The result has one row per group: the group key column(s) followed by the aggregated columns. Parameters: # parameter *aggsIntoExpr | Iterable[IntoExpr] (int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None | Iterable[int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None]) Aggregation expressions to compute per group. # parameter **named_aggsIntoExpr (int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None) Aggregation expressions as keyword arguments, where the keyword names the output column. Example: tf.group_by("k").agg(col("v").sum().alias("s")) tf.group_by("k").agg(col("v").mean().alias("m"))

method len def len(name: str | None = None) -> TableFrame Count the rows in each group. Safe on any TableFrame (it counts rows, not column values). Parameters: # parameter namestr | None Name for the count column (default "len"). Example: tf.group_by("g").len() Name the output column to keep it distinct from the data: tf.group_by("g").len("rows")

method count def count() -> TableFrame Count the non-null values of each column within each group. Yields one count column per non-key column. Safe on any TableFrame (it counts values, not reduces them). Example: tf.group_by("g").count()

method max def max() -> TableFrame Take the maximum of each non-key column within each group. Reduces EVERY column; may fail on a table's hidden system columns through storage. Prefer agg(col(...).max()). Example: tf.group_by("g").agg(col("a").max().alias("largest"))

method mean def mean() -> TableFrame Average each non-key column within each group. Reduces EVERY column; may fail on a table's hidden system columns through storage. Prefer agg(col(...).mean()). Example: tf.group_by("g").agg(col("a").mean().alias("average"))

method median def median() -> TableFrame Take the median of each non-key column within each group. Reduces EVERY column; may fail on a table's hidden system columns through storage. Prefer agg(col(...).median()). Example: tf.group_by("g").agg(col("a").median().alias("middle"))

method min def min() -> TableFrame Take the minimum of each non-key column within each group. Reduces EVERY column; may fail on a table's hidden system columns through storage. Prefer agg(col(...).min()). Example: tf.group_by("g").agg(col("a").min().alias("smallest"))

method n_unique def n_unique() -> TableFrame Count the distinct values of each non-key column within each group. Reduces EVERY column; may fail on a table's hidden system columns through storage. Prefer agg(col(...).n_unique()). Example: tf.group_by("g").agg(col("a").n_unique().alias("distinct"))

method sum def sum() -> TableFrame Sum each non-key column within each group. Reduces EVERY column; may fail on a table's hidden system columns through storage. Prefer agg(col(...).sum()). Example: tf.group_by("g").agg(col("a").sum().alias("total"))

Values whose predicate is not True (including null) are dropped. Typically used inside an aggregation. Parameters: # parameter *predicatesIntoExprColumn | Iterable[IntoExprColumn] (Expr | str | Iterable[Expr | str]) Boolean expressions to apply. # parameter **constraintsAny column=value keyword filters, combined with predicates using logical and. Example: tf.group_by("g").agg( col("a").filter(col("a") > 1).sum().alias("big_total"), )

method and_ def and_(*others: Any = ()) -> Expr Bitwise and with the given expressions (integer or boolean). Parameters: # parameter *othersAny Expressions to combine with logical/bitwise and. Example: tf.filter(col("flag").and_(col("a") > 2))

Example: tf.select(col("v").eq(None).alias("eq")) # null everywhere tf.select(col("v").eq_missing(None).alias("eq_missing")) # True on nulls

method ge def ge(other: Any) -> Expr Element-wise greater-than-or-equal, like expr >= other. Parameters: # parameter otherAny Value or expression to compare against. Example: tf.filter(col("a").ge(2))
method gt def gt(other: Any) -> Expr Element-wise greater-than, like expr > other. Parameters: # parameter otherAny Value or expression to compare against. Example: tf.filter(col("a").gt(2))
method le def le(other: Any) -> Expr Element-wise less-than-or-equal, like expr <= other. Parameters: # parameter otherAny Value or expression to compare against. Example: tf.filter(col("a").le(2))

Parameters: # parameter exponentIntoExprColumn | int | float (Expr | str | int | float) Value or expression to use as the exponent. Example: tf.select(col("a").pow(2).alias("squared"))

Parameters: # parameter otherExpr | Collection[Any] Collection or expression of allowed values. # parameter nulls_equalbool If True, a null element matches a null in other. Example: tf.filter(col("a").is_between(2, 4)) Both bounds are inclusive by default; closed narrows them: tf.filter(col("a").is_between(2, 4, closed="left"))

Parameters: # parameter seedint Base seed for the hash. # parameter seed_1int | None Optional additional seed. # parameter seed_2int | None Optional additional seed. # parameter seed_3int | None Optional additional seed. Reinterprets the raw bits (no value conversion); for a real conversion use cast. Only valid on 64-bit integer columns. Parameters: # parameter signedbool | None If True reinterpret as signed, if False as unsigned. # parameter dtypePolarsDataType | None (DataType | None) Explicit target integer type; overrides signed. Example: tf.select(col("a").reinterpret(signed=False).alias("bits"))

Parameters: # parameter methodRankMethod (Literal['average', 'min', 'max', 'dense', 'ordinal', 'random']) Tie-handling method: average (default), min, max, dense, ordinal or random. # parameter descendingbool If True, rank from largest to smallest. # parameter seedint | None Random seed, used only when method is random. Example: tf.with_columns(col("a").rank().alias("position")) method decides how ties are resolved, and descending ranks the largest value first: tf.with_columns(col("a").rank("dense", descending=True).alias("place"))

Order-dependent, so sort first for a deterministic result. Parameters: # parameter nint | IntoExpr (int | int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None) Rows to look back; negative looks forward. # parameter null_behaviorNullBehavior (Literal['ignore', 'drop']) How to handle nulls: ignore or drop. TableFrame class class TableFrame Bases: EngineFrame Categories: tableframe A lazy, immutable tabular frame -- Tabsdata's wrapper over polars LazyFrame. Every operation returns a new TableFrame without mutating the input. Instances arrive as arguments (and are returned) in @publisher / @transformer / @subscriber functions; build one directly with TableFrame.from_polars / from_pandas / from_dict / empty. Reference columns with col and constants with lit (both from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions).

Every operation returns a new TableFrame without mutating the input. Instances arrive as arguments (and are returned) in @publisher / @transformer / @subscriber functions; build one directly with TableFrame.from_polars / from_pandas / from_dict / empty. Reference columns with col and constants with lit (both from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions).
tf = TableFrame.from_dict({"g": ["x", "y", "x"], "v": [1, 2, 3]}) tf.filter(col("v") > 1).group_by("g").agg(col("v").sum().alias("total"))

method explain def explain( *, format: ExplainFormat = 'plain', optimized: bool = True, type_coercion: bool = True, predicate_pushdown: bool = True, projection_pushdown: bool = True, simplify_expression: bool = True, slice_pushdown: bool = True, comm_subplan_elim: bool = True, comm_subexpr_elim: bool = True, cluster_with_columns: bool = True, collapse_joins: bool = True, streaming: bool = False, engine: EngineType = 'auto', tree_format: bool | None = None, optimizations: Any = ..., ) -> str Return the query plan of this TableFrame as text. The remaining boolean flags each toggle one query-plan optimization (predicate/projection pushdown, common-subplan elimination, ...); leave them at their defaults unless diagnosing the plan. Parameters: # parameter formatExplainFormat (Literal['plain', 'tree']) "plain" or "tree" rendering. # parameter optimizedbool Show the optimized plan (default) rather than the raw logical plan. # parameter type_coercionbool # parameter predicate_pushdownbool # parameter projection_pushdownbool # parameter simplify_expressionbool # parameter slice_pushdownbool # parameter comm_subplan_elimbool # parameter comm_subexpr_elimbool # parameter cluster_with_columnsbool # parameter collapse_joinsbool # parameter streamingbool Show the plan for streaming execution. # parameter engineEngineType (Literal['auto', 'in-memory', 'streaming', 'gpu']) Target engine -- "auto", "in-memory", "streaming" or "gpu". # parameter tree_formatbool | None # parameter optimizationsAny Example: tf.filter(col("a") > 2).explain() The tree rendering is easier to read for a deep plan: tf.explain(format="tree")

method show_graph def show_graph( *, optimized: bool = True, show: bool = True, output_path: str | Path | None = None, raw_output: bool = False, figsize: tuple[float, float] = (16.0, 12.0), type_coercion: bool = True, _type_check: bool = True, predicate_pushdown: bool = True, projection_pushdown: bool = True, simplify_expression: bool = True, slice_pushdown: bool = True, comm_subplan_elim: bool = True, comm_subexpr_elim: bool = True, cluster_with_columns: bool = True, collapse_joins: bool = True, engine: EngineType = 'auto', plan_stage: PlanStage = 'ir', _check_order: bool = True, optimizations: Any = ..., ) -> str | None Render the query plan of this TableFrame as a graph. The remaining boolean flags toggle individual query-plan optimizations; leave them at their defaults unless diagnosing the plan. method inspect def inspect(fmt: str = '{}') -> TableFrame Print this TableFrame mid-chain and pass it through unchanged. Handy for debugging a chained pipeline: it returns the same TableFrame so it can sit between other operations. Parameters: # parameter fmtstr Format string applied to the printed frame. Example: tf.filter(col("a") > 1).inspect().select("a", "b")

method sort def sort( by: IntoExpr | Iterable[IntoExpr], *more_by: IntoExpr = (), descending: bool | Sequence[bool] = False, nulls_last: bool | Sequence[bool] = False, maintain_order: bool = False, multithreaded: bool = True, ) -> TableFrame Sort the rows by one or more columns or expressions. Parameters: # parameter byIntoExpr | Iterable[IntoExpr] (int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None | Iterable[int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None]) Column name(s) or expression(s) to sort by. # parameter *more_byIntoExpr (int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None) Additional sort keys, as positional arguments. # parameter descendingbool | Sequence[bool] Sort descending; a single bool, or one per sort key. # parameter nulls_lastbool | Sequence[bool] Place nulls last; a single bool, or one per sort key. # parameter maintain_orderbool Keep the input order of tied rows. # parameter multithreadedbool Example: tf.sort("k", descending=True) tf.sort(["k", "n"], descending=[True, False])

method cast def cast( dtypes: Mapping[ColumnNameOrSelector | PolarsDataType, PolarsDataType | PythonDataType] | PolarsDataType | Schema, *, strict: bool = True, ) -> TableFrame Cast columns to new data types. Data types come from tabsdatak.tableframe.datatypes. Parameters: # parameter dtypesMapping[ColumnNameOrSelector | PolarsDataType, PolarsDataType | PythonDataType] | PolarsDataType | Schema (Mapping[str | Any | DataType, DataType | type[int] | type[float] | type[bool] | type[str] | type[date] | type[time] | type[datetime] | type[timedelta] | type[list[Any]] | type[tuple[Any, ...]] | type[bytes] | type[object] | type[Decimal] | type[None]] | DataType | Schema) A single data type applied to every column, a mapping of column (name or selector) to its target data type, or a Schema. # parameter strictbool If True (default), raise when a value cannot be cast; if False, unconvertible values become null. Example: tf.cast({"a": Float64, "b": String}) tf.cast({"id": Int8}, strict=False)

method clear def clear(n: int = 0) -> TableFrame Return a frame with the same schema but no data. Parameters: # parameter nint Number of all-null rows to produce. 0 (default) yields a zero-row frame; a positive n yields n rows of nulls. Example: tf.clear() A positive n keeps the schema and yields that many all-null rows: tf.clear(3)

method filter def filter( *predicates: IntoExprColumn | Iterable[IntoExprColumn] | bool | list[bool] = (), **constraints: Any = {}, ) -> TableFrame Keep only the rows matching every given predicate. Parameters: # parameter *predicatesIntoExprColumn | Iterable[IntoExprColumn] | bool | list[bool] (Expr | str | Iterable[Expr | str] | bool | list[bool]) Boolean expressions; a row is kept only if it satisfies ALL of them (they are AND-ed together). # parameter **constraintsAny Column-equality shortcuts as keyword arguments -- filter(g="x") means filter(col("g") == "x"). Example: tf.filter(col("a") > 2) tf.filter((col("a") > 1) & (col("a") < 5)) tf.filter(col("g").is_in(["x", "y"])) tf.filter(g="x")

method select def select( *exprs: IntoExpr | Iterable[IntoExpr] = (), **named_exprs: IntoExpr = {}, ) -> TableFrame Select and/or derive columns, dropping every other column. Parameters: # parameter *exprsIntoExpr | Iterable[IntoExpr] (int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None | Iterable[int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None]) Column names or expressions to keep; each expression becomes a column (name it with Expr.alias). # parameter **named_exprsIntoExpr (int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None) Expressions as keyword arguments, where the keyword is the output column name. Example: tf.select("a", "b") tf.select((col("a") * 2).alias("a2")) tf.select(a2=col("a") * 2)

method group_by def group_by( *by: IntoExpr | Iterable[IntoExpr] = (), maintain_order: bool = False, **named_by: IntoExpr = {}, ) -> LazyGroupBy Group rows by one or more keys for aggregation. Returns a LazyGroupBy; call .agg(...) on it with reducing expressions to produce one row per group. Prefer agg(col(...).<reduction>()) over the LazyGroupBy reduction shortcuts (see LazyGroupBy). Parameters: # parameter *byIntoExpr | Iterable[IntoExpr] (int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None | Iterable[int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None]) Column name(s) or expression(s) to group by. # parameter maintain_orderbool Emit groups in the order they first appear. # parameter **named_byIntoExpr (int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None) Grouping expressions as keyword arguments, where the keyword names the group column. Example: tf.group_by("k").agg(col("v").sum().alias("s"))

method join def join( other: TableFrame, on: str | Expr | Sequence[str | Expr] | None = None, how: JoinStrategy = 'inner', *, left_on: str | Expr | Sequence[str | Expr] | None = None, right_on: str | Expr | Sequence[str | Expr] | None = None, suffix: str = '_right', ) -> TableFrame Join this TableFrame with another on one or more keys. #MANUAL CHANGE POST GEN: dropped the generated params validate, nulls_equal, coalesce, maintain_order, allow_parallel, force_parallel -- the runtime does not accept them (TypeError). Parameters: # parameter otherTableFrame The right TableFrame to join with. # parameter onstr | Expr | Sequence[str | Expr] | None Key column(s) present in BOTH frames. Use this OR left_on/right_on, never both; omit it for how="cross". # parameter howJoinStrategy (Literal['inner', 'left', 'right', 'full', 'semi', 'anti', 'cross', 'outer']) Join strategy -- one of "inner", "left", "right", "full" (a.k.a. "outer"), "cross", "semi" or "anti". "semi" keeps left rows that have a match, "anti" keeps those that do not, and "cross" is the cartesian product (takes no keys). # parameter left_onstr | Expr | Sequence[str | Expr] | None Key column(s) on the left frame, paired positionally with right_on when the join keys have different names. # parameter right_onstr | Expr | Sequence[str | Expr] | None Key column(s) on the right frame; use with left_on. # parameter suffixstr Suffix added to right-frame columns whose names collide with the left frame (default "_right"). Example: left.join(right, on="id", how="inner") left.join(right, left_on="id", right_on="rid") left.join(right, how="cross")

method with_columns def with_columns( *exprs: IntoExpr | Iterable[IntoExpr] = (), **named_exprs: IntoExpr = {}, ) -> TableFrame Add or replace columns, keeping all existing ones. Like select but non-destructive: the given expressions are added, and any whose name matches an existing column replaces it in place. Parameters: # parameter *exprsIntoExpr | Iterable[IntoExpr] (int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None | Iterable[int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None]) Expressions to add; name each with Expr.alias. # parameter **named_exprsIntoExpr (int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None) Expressions as keyword arguments, where the keyword is the output column name. Example: tf.with_columns((col("a") + 1).alias("c")) tf.with_columns(c=col("a") + col("b"))

method drop def drop( *columns: ColumnNameOrSelector | Iterable[ColumnNameOrSelector] = (), strict: bool = True, ) -> TableFrame Remove the named columns. Parameters: # parameter *columnsColumnNameOrSelector | Iterable[ColumnNameOrSelector] (str | Any | Iterable[str | Any]) Column name(s) or selector(s) to drop, as several positional arguments or a single list. # parameter strictbool If True (default), raise when a named column is missing; if False, silently ignore missing names. Example: tf.drop("a", "b") tf.drop(["b", "c"])

method rename def rename( mapping: Mapping[str, str] | Callable[[str], str], *, strict: bool = True, ) -> TableFrame Rename columns. #VERIFY: the callable form (a function over column names) has a known system-column divergence (xp failing sub-suite); the dict form is the reliable one. Parameters: # parameter mappingMapping[str, str] | Callable[[str], str] A dict of {old_name: new_name} (the reliable form), or a callable applied to each existing column name to produce its new name. # parameter strictbool If True (default), raise when a key in mapping is not an existing column. Example: tf.rename({"a": "x", "b": "y"})

method slice def slice(offset: int, length: int | None = None) -> TableFrame Return length rows starting at row offset. Parameters: # parameter offsetint Zero-based index of the first row to keep. # parameter lengthint | None Number of rows to keep; None keeps all rows from offset to the end. Example: tf.slice(1, 2) # two rows, starting at the second Omit the length to take everything from offset on: tf.slice(2)
method limit def limit(n: int = 5) -> TableFrame Return the first n rows (an alias of head). Parameters: # parameter nint Number of rows to keep. Example: tf.limit(3)
method head def head(n: int = 5) -> TableFrame Return the first n rows. Parameters: # parameter nint Number of rows to keep. Example: tf.head(3)
method tail def tail(n: int = 5) -> TableFrame Return the last n rows. Parameters: # parameter nint Number of rows to keep. Example: tf.tail(3)
method last def last() -> TableFrame Return the last row as a one-row TableFrame. Example: tf.sort("id").last()
method first def first() -> TableFrame Return the first row as a one-row TableFrame. Example: tf.sort("id").first()

method fill_null def fill_null( value: Any | Expr | None = None, strategy: FillNullStrategy | None = None, limit: int | None = None, *, matches_supertype: bool = True, ) -> TableFrame Replace null values with a value or a fill strategy. Provide either value or strategy, not both. Parameters: # parameter valueAny | Expr | None Value (or expression) to substitute for nulls. # parameter strategyFillNullStrategy | None (Literal['forward', 'backward', 'min', 'max', 'mean', 'zero', 'one'] | None) Fill rule instead of a value -- one of "forward", "backward", "min", "max", "mean", "zero" or "one". # parameter limitint | None With "forward" / "backward", the maximum number of consecutive nulls to fill. # parameter matches_supertypebool Cast the fill value to the column's supertype when their types differ. Example: tf.fill_null(0) tf.sort("id").fill_null(strategy="forward", limit=1)

method fill_nan def fill_nan(value: int | float | Expr | None) -> TableFrame Replace floating-point NaN values with the given value. Targets NaN entries in float columns -- distinct from fill_null, which replaces nulls. Parameters: # parameter valueint | float | Expr | None Value (or expression) to substitute for NaN. Example: tf.fill_nan(0.0)

Parameters: # parameter subsetIntoExpr | Collection[IntoExpr] | None (int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None | Collection[int | float | Decimal | date | time | datetime | timedelta | str | bool | bytes | list[Any] | Expr | str | None] | None) Column(s) whose values define a duplicate; pass this explicitly. When omitted, all columns are considered. # parameter keepUniqueKeepStrategy (Literal['first', 'last', 'any', 'none']) Which duplicate to keep -- "any" (default, fastest), "first", "last" or "none" (drop every duplicated row). # parameter maintain_orderbool Preserve the input row order. Example: tf.unique(subset="a") tf.unique(subset="k", keep="last")

Parameters: # parameter subsetColumnNameOrSelector | Collection[ColumnNameOrSelector] | None (str | Any | Collection[str | Any] | None) Column(s) to check for NaN; when omitted, all columns are considered. Example: tf.drop_nans("v") Omit the subset to drop a row when any float column holds NaN: tf.drop_nans()

Parameters: # parameter subsetColumnNameOrSelector | Collection[ColumnNameOrSelector] | None (str | Any | Collection[str | Any] | None) Column(s) to check for nulls; when omitted, all columns are considered. method unnest def unnest( columns: ColumnNameOrSelector | Collection[ColumnNameOrSelector], *more_columns: ColumnNameOrSelector = (), separator: str | None = None, ) -> TableFrame Expand struct columns into one column per field. Each named struct column is replaced, in place, by its fields as top-level columns. Parameters: # parameter columnsColumnNameOrSelector | Collection[ColumnNameOrSelector] (str | Any | Collection[str | Any]) Struct column(s) to expand. # parameter *more_columnsColumnNameOrSelector (str | Any) Additional struct columns, as positional arguments. # parameter separatorstr | None If given, prefix each new column with its parent name and this separator to avoid name clashes. Example: tf.unnest("s") tf.unnest("s", "t")

method grok def grok( expr: str | Expr, pattern: str, schema: Mapping[str, ColumnDefinition], ) -> TableFrame Parse unstructured text into columns with a Grok pattern. Matches pattern against a string column and appends one column per named capture, keeping every existing column. A row whose text does not match gets null in each new column, so a bad line never fails the read. ColumnDefinition (from tabsdatak.tableframe.grok) names each new column and gives its data type. Parameters: # parameter exprstr | Expr Name of the string column to parse, or an expression resolving to one. # parameter patternstr Grok pattern whose named captures (%{WORD:user}) become the new columns. # parameter schemaMapping[str, ColumnDefinition] Mapping of capture name to the ColumnDefinition describing the column it produces. A definition whose name differs from the capture renames the output column; its dtype is what the captured text is parsed into. Returns: A new TableFrame with one column added per capture. Example: tf.grok( "logs", r"%{WORD:user}-%{WORD:action}-%{INT:year}", { "user": ColumnDefinition("user", String), "action": ColumnDefinition("action", String), "year": ColumnDefinition("year", Int64), }, ) A definition can rename the capture, and the source column may be given as an expression: tf.grok( col("logs"), r"%{WORD:user}-.*", {"user": ColumnDefinition("who", String)}, ) When a pattern repeats a capture name, the extra columns are disambiguated with a numeric suffix (field, field[1]).

method from_polars def from_polars(data = None, schema = None) -> TableFrame Build a TableFrame from a polars frame. Takes a polars DataFrame or LazyFrame; any other input type raises. The system columns are seeded on top of the given data. Parameters: # parameter data The polars DataFrame or LazyFrame to wrap. None yields an empty frame. # parameter schema Optional {column: data type} mapping to cast the data to; the data keeps its own types when omitted. Returns: A new TableFrame over the given data. Example: TableFrame.from_polars(pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})) TableFrame.from_polars(pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}))

method from_pandas def from_pandas(data = None, schema = None) -> TableFrame Build a TableFrame from a pandas DataFrame. Parameters: # parameter data The pandas DataFrame to convert. None yields an empty frame. # parameter schema Optional {column: data type} mapping to cast the data to; the types pandas inferred are kept when omitted. Returns: A new TableFrame over the given data. Example: TableFrame.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}))

method from_dict def from_dict(data = None, schema = None) -> TableFrame Build a TableFrame from a {column: values} dict. Every value list must have the same length -- one entry per row. Parameters: # parameter data Mapping of column name to the column's values. None yields an empty frame. # parameter schema Optional {column: data type} mapping to cast the columns to; types are inferred from the values when omitted. Returns: A new TableFrame over the given data. Example: TableFrame.from_dict({"g": ["x", "y"], "v": [1, 2]}) Pin the column types instead of having them inferred: TableFrame.from_dict({"v": [1, 2]}, schema={"v": Float64})

method empty def empty(schema = None) -> TableFrame Build a TableFrame with no rows. Parameters: # parameter schema Optional {column: data type} mapping giving the frame its columns. Without it the frame has no columns either. Returns: A new, empty TableFrame. Example: TableFrame.empty(schema={"id": Int64, "name": String}) With no schema the result has neither rows nor columns -- useful as the starting point of a concat: TableFrame.empty()

method extract_one def extract_one( with_connector_columns: bool = False, fail_if_empty: bool = False, ) -> dict[str, DataType | None] | None Return the only row as a column-to-value dictionary. Internal columns are always dropped; connector columns are kept only when with_connector_columns is set. Fails if the TableFrame has more than one row. Returns None when the TableFrame is empty, unless fail_if_empty is set, in which case it fails. Parameters: # parameter with_connector_columnsbool Keep the connector columns a source attached to the row instead of dropping them. # parameter fail_if_emptybool Raise instead of returning None when there is no row to extract. Returns: The row as {column: value}, or None when the frame is Example: tf.filter(col("id") == 1).extract_one() Reading a single aggregate out of a frame is the common use: tf.select(col("v").sum().alias("total")).extract_one()

method max_for def max_for( *cols: str = (), fail_if_empty: bool = False, ) -> dict[str, DataType | None] | None Return the given columns of the row that ranks highest by them. Each column is compared in its own natural order (numbers numerically, dates chronologically, strings alphabetically). The columns are ordered comparison keys: the first is primary, each subsequent one breaks ties on the previous. Returns None when the TableFrame is empty, unless fail_if_empty is set, in which case it fails. Parameters: # parameter *colsstr Columns to rank by, in priority order; the same columns are the ones returned. # parameter fail_if_emptybool Raise instead of returning None when the frame has no rows. Returns: The named columns of the top-ranking row as {column: value}, Example: tf.max_for("v") With several keys the later ones break ties on the earlier: tf.max_for("g", "v")

method min_for def min_for( *cols: str = (), fail_if_empty: bool = False, ) -> dict[str, DataType | None] | None Return the given columns of the row that ranks lowest by them. Each column is compared in its own natural order (numbers numerically, dates chronologically, strings alphabetically). The columns are ordered comparison keys: the first is primary, each subsequent one breaks ties on the previous. Returns None when the TableFrame is empty, unless fail_if_empty is set, in which case it fails. Parameters: # parameter *colsstr Columns to rank by, in priority order; the same columns are the ones returned. # parameter fail_if_emptybool Raise instead of returning None when the frame has no rows. Returns: The named columns of the bottom-ranking row as Example: tf.min_for("v") A cursor over an incremental read is the common use -- the lowest unprocessed key: tf.filter(col("processed").not_()).min_for("id")
